section_summary: This section centers on the 1948 dispute over a Japanese Cabinet order restricting collective bargaining and strikes by government employees. State Department records include competing assessments from Japanese, American, and British officials, accounts of James S. Killen’s resignation, and discussions of how to revise the policy. It also contains a lengthy English–Japanese labor terminology list and brief telegrams on labor conditions, Soviet criticism, and Japanese employment in China.

subfiles.title: Communist Influence in Japanese Labor
subfiles.doc_type: memorandum of conversation; enclosure to despatch no. 490
subfiles.about: Hitotsumatsu Maseji discusses communist influence, labor rights, and Occupation economic policy.
subfiles.summary: Hitotsumatsu argues that Occupation policy has favored labor over management and strengthened communist influence in unions. He welcomes restrictions on government workers’ strikes, criticizes earlier SCAP labor policy and economic controls, and fears depression and unrest after the Occupation.

subfiles.title: Draft Telegram to SCAP Regarding Rights of Japanese Government Employees
subfiles.about: Requests clearance of a joint message challenging the Japanese Cabinet’s labor order.
subfiles.summary: Seeks approval to send the draft through Army channels to SCAP.

subfiles.title: Draft Telegram to SCAP Regarding Rights of Japanese Government Employees
subfiles.about: A second copy requests clearance of the proposed joint message to SCAP.
subfiles.summary: Duplicates the recommendation and attachment list on page 56.

subfiles.title: Draft Telegram to SCAP on the July 31 Cabinet Order
subfiles.from: Departments of Labor, State, and Army
subfiles.about: Urges restoration of bargaining rights for government industrial workers and asks SCAP’s plans.
subfiles.summary: The draft says the ordinance exceeds MacArthur’s letter and conflicts with U.S. and FEC policy. It recommends collective bargaining for industrial employees, limited strike rights, and binding arbitration where stoppages threaten the public interest.

subfiles.title: Letter Transmitting Draft Message to SCAP
subfiles.about: Requests urgent Army clearance and dispatch of the joint labor policy message.
subfiles.summary: Transmits the coordinated State–Labor draft to the Army for early action.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Draft Telegram to SCAP
subfiles.about: Explains Labor Department support and anticipated international reaction to the Cabinet order.
subfiles.summary: Reports Gibson’s concern, hopes SCAP can prompt revision, and notes British and European labor criticism.

subfiles.title: Collective Bargaining and Strike Rights of Japanese Government Employees
subfiles.about: Assesses the Cabinet order against U.S. and FEC labor policy.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum argues that the order removes bargaining and strike rights from a broad group of government industrial workers, beyond ordinary civil servants. It urges a State Department position and warns of objections from FEC governments and U.S. labor organizations.

subfiles.title: Japanese Cabinet Order Relative to Rights of Government Employees
subfiles.about: Sets temporary restrictions on collective bargaining, strikes, and dispute tactics by public employees.
subfiles.summary: The order permits employees to present grievances but removes coercive collective bargaining and prohibits strikes or tactics impairing government operations. It suspends pending mediation and provides penalties, pending legislation by the Diet.

subfiles.title: Labor Standards Violations in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Relays a news report of widespread violations of Japanese labor standards.
subfiles.summary: Reports violations in more than 1,900 of 2,200 Tokyo workshops inspected.

subfiles.title: Japanese Government Ordinance Regarding Rights of Public Employees
subfiles.about: Records British concerns conveyed privately by J. F. Ford.
subfiles.summary: Ford says Britain shares Australian concern about the ordinance but avoided a public Allied Council debate amid Soviet intervention. He asks for remedial measures before Parliament reconvenes; U.S. officials promise consideration and transmission to SCAP.

subfiles.title: British Views on the July 31 Ordinance
subfiles.about: Objects to denying industrial workers bargaining and strike rights and limiting civil servants to petition.
subfiles.summary: Urges SCAP to secure better bargaining arrangements for industrial workers and civil servants.

subfiles.title: Yesterday’s Meeting on Japanese Labor Situation
subfiles.about: Reports interdepartmental decisions on a press release and principles for Japanese government workers’ rights.
subfiles.summary: Reports Labor–Army disagreement and tentative Army acceptance that the ordinance withdrew bargaining rights too broadly.

subfiles.title: Attached Memorandum of Conversation with Mr. Killen
subfiles.about: Introduces Killen’s account of SCAP’s decision and his resignation.
subfiles.summary: Attributes MacArthur’s decision largely to anticommunist arguments advanced by Hoover and Whitney.

subfiles.title: Denial of Collective Bargaining and Strike Rights of Japanese Government and Public Employees
subfiles.about: Records James S. Killen’s account of SCAP’s labor policy decision and its effects.
subfiles.summary: Killen describes a Headquarters debate in which he advocated bargaining backed by mediation and arbitration, while Government Section officials argued for civil service restrictions. He says the July 22 letter was effectively a directive and that Whitney supplied the Japanese government with an implementation plan. Killen explains his resignation, reports protests across the labor movement, and warns that suppression of union rights could strengthen communist organizers. He proposes guidance, administrative reforms, and limited legislation to help develop independent union leadership.

subfiles.title: Word List of Labor Terminology
subfiles.from: Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards copies of an English–Japanese labor terminology list prepared by SCAP’s Labor Division.
subfiles.summary: Highlights six labor terms whose Japanese translations frequently cause confusion.

subfiles.title: Word List of Labor Terminology, Second Edition
subfiles.from: Labor Division, Economic and Scientific Section, SCAP
subfiles.about: Defines and translates labor relations and employment terms for use in Japan.
subfiles.summary: An introductory note explains translation problems involving local unions, management councils, collective bargaining, grievance procedures, conciliation, mediation, arbitration, and closed shops. The alphabetical glossary then pairs English terms with romanized Japanese and Japanese script, covering union organization, labor law, wages, employment, disputes, and workplace conditions.

subfiles.title: Pravda Report on Soviet Criticism of Japanese Labor Restrictions
subfiles.about: Reports Pravda’s account of a Soviet proposal to revoke the strike restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Says Pravda quoted Panyushkin’s FEC criticism of MacArthur’s letter and the Japanese decree.

subfiles.title: Japanese Employment Abroad
subfiles.about: Discusses a Chinese request to employ Japanese technicians at a Guangdong paper mill.
subfiles.summary: Tsui asks about approval for 20 Japanese technicians to reinstall a paper mill near Guangzhou. Ray says SCAP may decide the matter, then asks whether China’s request signals a broader change in its restrictive position on Japanese travel abroad.

subfiles.title: Labor Policy in Japan
subfiles.about: Reviews the State–Labor–Army conference and whether to send State’s policy interpretation to the Army.
subfiles.summary: Recommends withholding the attached statement unless SCAP’s reply makes its transmission necessary.

subfiles.title: Routing Query on Communicating with the Army
subfiles.about: Asks whether the accompanying material needs to be communicated to the Army.
subfiles.summary: A brief handwritten query accompanies the preceding labor policy memorandum.
